headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors: shared project/workspace paths plus Windsurf’s clipboard/MCP and auto-execute surface can steer gpt-engineer’s file-writing loop.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a shared project directory and has no self-isolation by default; Windsurf shares state via local filesystem and can ingest clipboard/MCP content. That creates a default path for attacker-controlled project files or copied text to influence either agent’s instruction stream, though not as directly as a shared MCP server.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory or workspace files
IF content from that directory is treated as instructions by either agent
mitigations: Use separate project directories for each agent
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents
Require a human review step before either agent follows file content as instructions
Pin one agent to read-only access for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for files passed between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write project/workspace files, and both call external model APIs by default. gpt-engineer touches generated source code and Windsurf touches open files, so sensitive code or secrets in the shared workspace can flow to either backend during normal operation. The pair is not documented as isolated, so leakage risk is real.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared project/workspace
IF either agent sends file contents to its configured model backend
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Use separate workspaces for code and confidential material
Disable automatic file upload or context expansion where possible
Rotate any exposed API keys after a shared-session review
requires-engineering: enforce per-file redaction before model calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. Windsurf also modifies git state while gpt-engineer writes files in a project directory; with shared local state and no locking, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt repository state. This matches the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or project directory
IF both are allowed to write or run commands concurrently
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a given repo
Use separate clones or worktrees
Disable git-writing actions in one agent during the other’s session
Add a manual checkpoint before any commit or destructive shell command
requires-engineering: add file and git locks across agents

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer’s workflow is to write files then offer to run, while Windsurf’s Cascade can auto-execute commands subject to a setting. If Windsurf consumes gpt-engineer’s generated code or instructions without verification, an error can propagate into shell execution or repository changes. The pair therefore has a strong default cascade path.
conditions: IF Windsurf treats gpt-engineer output as authoritative input
IF auto-execute is enabled or command approval is bypassed
mitigations: Require explicit human verification of gpt-engineer output before Windsurf acts on it
Keep Windsurf auto-execute disabled
Limit gpt-engineer to generating patches, not runnable commands
Review any shell command generated from the other agent before execution
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Windsurf is closed-source and handles model-provider keys plus open files, while gpt-engineer is open-source and handles OPENAI_API_KEY and generated source code. If regulated or confidential code is placed in the shared workspace, the pair can create retention or residency mismatches through external model calls. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data, secrets, or customer code are stored in the shared workspace
IF either agent forwards that content to an external model provider
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use a separate non-regulated repo for agentic work
Remove secrets from prompts and files before sessions
Confirm vendor retention terms before processing sensitive code
requires-engineering: enforce data-class routing and retention controls
